title: Redwood discovery call with Solstice Payments - cost/unit economics
summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics and deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Customer has budget constraints and latency SLOs; asked for pricing comparison, recommended benchmark, and security docs. Agreed next step: Redwood to send pricing deck, run small benchmark (sample workload), and schedule dedicated follow-up with procurement and security.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
next_steps: Erin to send pricing deck and TCO spreadsheet by 2026-11-20
Samir to propose benchmark run config and schedule by 2026-11-22
Customer to confirm pilot budget and stakeholders (procurement + security) by 2026-11-25
action_items: Erin Patel | Send pricing deck + TCO sheet | 2026-11-20
Samir Kaur | Draft benchmark config (50 req/s, 10k token avg) and test plan | 2026-11-22
Maya Chen | Share representative prompts and token distribution csv | 2026-11-21
transcript: [00:00] Erin Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining from Solstice. quick roll call, I'll hand it to Samir for the deep-dive later.

[00:22] Daniel Reyes: Hi, Daniel here. Maya and Liam on. We're mainly trying to understand cost/unit economics — whether we go hosted or reserve capacity — and what that means for our monthly runrate.
[00:35] Maya Chen: yep, and we have a latency requirement, like p95 under 200 ms for our interactive flows. also curious about batching effects on cost vs latency.

[00:48] Erin Patel: Great context. high level, Redwood's hosted pricing is per-token with unit economics that vary by model and batching efficiency; Dedicated gives you committed throughput and lower per-token cost typically, and Private gives full control for compliance but has infra+license implications.
[01:10] Liam O'Sullivan: Quick question — when you say per-token, is that both input + output tokens? our cost modeling needs both sides included.

[01:22] Samir Kaur: yes both directions count. and one nuance: effective cost can drop significantly with batching and KV/prefix caching for chat-style workloads since repeated context tokens are cached in the KV cache and not recomputed server-side every time, so per-token billed vs executed tokens can differ a bit in practice — there's some subtlety depending on request patterns.
[01:55] Daniel Reyes: mmh, can you give a concrete example? like if we send 1k concurrent requests with avg 800 tokens, how does batching help?

[02:10] Samir Kaur: right — so with batching we can combine requests into larger micro-batches; that improves GPU utilization so per-token GPU cost drops. for instance, with batch sizes of 16-32 we often see 20-40% cost improvements on throughput workloads. but latency tradeoff depends on your tolerances and how long you're willing to wait to accumulate a batch.
[02:38] Maya Chen: is there an automated batching policy? we don't want to tune this forever.

[02:46] Samir Kaur: yep, Redwood has workload-aware batching and adaptive policies — by default we try to meet latency SLOs while maximizing batch sizes. also there's request-level hints so you can opt-in per-route.
[03:05] Liam O'Sullivan: and what about prefix caching / kv cache eviction — do we need sticky sessions or something?

[03:15] Samir Kaur: KV cache is kept per-model-worker; sticky routing helps but Redwood also supports transparent KV cache rehydration across workers; eviction policy is LRU-ish. for high reuse chat flows you'll see big gains.

[03:40] Daniel Reyes: budget-wise we have roughly $15k/month earmarked for inference initially. want to know if that's realistic for our expected usage — about 100 reqs/s during peak, average 600 tokens per user interaction, plus embeddings batch jobs daily.

[03:58] Erin Patel: that's helpful. based on rough math, hosted per-token rates vs committed reserved capacity can swing your monthly spend by 1.5x-3x depending on batching and token reuse. we'll run a sample TCO for your workload and show hosted vs dedicated vs private line items.

[04:20] Daniel Reyes: ok great. also security/compliance is big — SOC2 is required, SSO, KMS for key management, and audit logs for queries — do you support customer-managed keys for private deployments?

[04:33] Erin Patel: yes, Private supports KMS/HSM integration and customer-managed keys; Dedicated has KMS integrations too. hosted supports envelope encryption and we can discuss BYOK for enterprise plans, plus full audit logging and RBAC. I'll attach the security pack.
[04:50] Maya Chen: can we get SOC2 artifacts? procurement will ask for them.
[04:55] Erin Patel: absolutely. will include SOC2 report + pen test summary and the security whitepaper in the follow-up.
[05:06] Daniel Reyes: what's the timeline if we wanted to do a pilot? we're aiming for an internal launch in Q1, so procurement and legal will want a path to buy in December.

[05:17] Erin Patel: typical pilot starts with 4-6 week benchmark + PoC, but we can compress. for Dedicated we can provision reserved nodes within 2-3 weeks once terms are agreed; Private has longer lead time depending on on-prem access and network setup.
[05:33] Liam O'Sullivan: network-wise, we need VPC peering and private endpoints. do you support strict egress rules and IP allowlists?
[05:42] Samir Kaur: yes, Redwood Dedicated and Private support VPC peering, private endpoints, and allowlisted IP ranges. we also support per-customer network ACLs for Dedicated.
[05:56] Maya Chen: curious about quantization/accuracy tradeoffs; if we go smaller models or 8-bit quan, how do you advise balancing cost vs quality?

[06:10] Samir Kaur: Redwood Optimize recommends quantization profiles per workflow. e.g., 8-bit often gives 2x-3x throughput improvements with small latency on quality for many tasks; our eval harness can run your prompts and show quality delta so you can decide.
[06:32] Daniel Reyes: would you run that eval on our prompts or do we need to provide them?

[06:37] Samir Kaur: ideally you share representative prompts and reference outputs; we can also anonymize or redact PII. Samir (oops, that's me) will coordinate — we'll run a small eval and model comparison.
[06:55] [crosstalk] Maya Chen: we'll share samples after the call —

[07:00] Erin Patel: quick aside on pricing models — Hosted: per-token and simple to get started; Dedicated: monthly reserved capacity with lower per-token compute costs and predictable bills; Private: license + infra costs, better for regulated data. we'll include example line-items in the TCO spreadsheet.
[07:22] Daniel Reyes: do you have a simple calc for monthly cost with 100 req/s and 600 tokens avg?

[07:29] Erin Patel: rough napkin — if hosted rate is X per 1k tokens, and you do 100r/s * 600 tokens * 3600s * peak-hours, it adds up. we'll plug your exact numbers and show sensitivity to batching, cache hit rate, and model choice in the sheet.
[07:49] Liam O'Sullivan: model choice is key — we sometimes can use a smaller model for embeddings and a large one for generation. do you support model routing/fallbacks?
[07:58] Samir Kaur: yes policy-based routing: latency-first vs cost-first, and automatic fallback to compatible variants if capacity constrained. plus we support A/B rollouts and canary traffic.
[08:12] Maya Chen: procurement will also ask about SLAs — what are your p99 latency SLOs for Dedicated vs Hosted?

[08:20] Erin Patel: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed latency and uptime targets in enterprise plans; hosted has published latency percentiles for each model in the catalog. we'll share the latency dashboards and sample traces.
[08:34] Daniel Reyes: are there penalties or credits if you miss the SLOs?
[08:38] Erin Patel: for Dedicated Enterprise contracts we include credits tied to availability SLAs. we'll put that in the commercial deck for review.
[08:49] [00:09:00] Daniel Reyes: sorry, just to double-check — when you talk about caching, are we billed for tokens that are cached?

[09:06] Samir Kaur: good Q. billing is per-token consumed by the model; if the KV cache avoids recomputation then effectively fewer tokens are executed and that lowers cost. however, input tokens are always counted for billing; there's some nuance around server-side dedupe for repeated system prompts — we'll detail it in the pricing doc.
[09:32] Maya Chen: would you help with modeling cost if we add a reranking step — embeddings and then a gen for top results? embeddings are batched nightly but need to be in our monthly calc.

[09:44] Erin Patel: yes, include batch jobs. embeddings are usually cheaper per token but can be heavy on throughput; we typically separate batch embedding cost and interactive generation cost in the TCO.
[09:58] Daniel Reyes: any hidden fees? e.g., storage for KV caches or additional observability charges?

[10:06] Erin Patel: observability retention and advanced logs are add-ons; basic tracing and token-level cost breakdowns are included. we'll call out optional add-ons in the pricing deck so you can see line items.
[10:20] Liam O'Sullivan: from infra perspective, provisioning Dedicated — how long to scale up if usage suddenly spikes beyond commit?

[10:29] Samir Kaur: Dedicated has burst capacity options; autoscaling policies can be configured but it depends on committed pool size. in emergencies we can failover to hosted capacity as a fallback to keep you online, though egress rules and data residency need consideration.
[10:47] Daniel Reyes: interesting. we need clear runbook for fallbacks because we're in payments and can't risk outages.
[10:53] Erin Patel: agree. we'll include a proposed fallback runbook and SLA integration points in the follow-up.
[11:02] Maya Chen: timeline — procurement wants a vendor shortlist by Nov 30. can you commit to delivering the benchmark results in two weeks?
[11:11] Samir Kaur: we can run a focused benchmark in ~7 business days if you provide sample prompts and approve the test configuration; results and a short TCO should be ready in 10 business days.
[11:25] Daniel Reyes: ok that works. we'll aim to share sample prompts and token distribution by 2026-11-21.

[11:33] Erin Patel: perfect. final recap — we will: send pricing deck + SOC2/security pack (Erin), propose benchmark config and schedule (Samir), customer will share prompts and confirm budget and stakeholders. follow-up meeting to review results scheduled after benchmarks.
[11:51] Maya Chen: one smaller ask — can you show an example config where batching is tuned to keep p95 < 200ms?
[11:58] Samir Kaur: yes we'll include a sample batching policy and expected latency vs cost curves in the benchmark report.
[12:07] Daniel Reyes: awesome, thanks everyone. that clarifies a lot. we'll review the docs when they come through.
[12:15] Erin Patel: thanks all — I'll email the artifacts and next steps. talk soon.
[12:20] [call end]

Note: transcript has occasional auto-transcription errors and speaker attribution may be approximate; shared artifacts referenced: pricing-deck.pdf (link), security-pack.zip (link), benchmark-sheet.csv (link).
